title: Mutate 'Em All and See If You Can Sort 'Em Out
body_text: As much as I love an experiment designed to slice and dice the possible explanations in one smooth motion, I also have always enjoyed the blue-sky “I wonder what would happen if. . .” kinds as well. And the modern era of molecular biology and computation really gives people the tools to do that sort of thing, as this recent preprint illustrates. What If. . .you took a simple virus and mutated every single one of the letters in its genetic code, one by one? What if you made sure along the way that you’d altered every single amino acid in all of the proteins being coded for? What would happen then? That’s what these authors did, with the extremely-well-studied bacteriophage ϕX174, which has single-stranded DNA. That was the first whole genome ever to be sequenced (by Fred Sanger et al. back in 1977), as well as the first to be chemically synthesized. It has 5,386 bases encoding 11 proteins (six structural and five non-structural); bacteriophages can run pretty lean. What they found was that about half of the single nucleotide variants reduced fitness (which, to be sure, means that half didn’t!) About 60% of those impairments showed a greater than 50% reduction in fitness. Mutations in protein coding regions were much more likely to be trouble, although 19% of mutations in noncoding regions also had bad effects. The great majority of those were in obvious regulatory elements (promoter sequences, ribosome binding sites, and so on). From the protein end of things, a particular scaffold protein and a particular capsid protein were the least tolerant of being messed around with. At the other end of the scale is the viral Protein K, in which no mutations seemed to affect fitness at all (!) Overall, about half of the detrimental mutations are in protein interface zones, with the next biggest group being protein core regions. Interestingly, AI-based predictors of mutational sensitivity did not do a very good job reproducing these numbers at all. It may be (as the authors note) that there haven’t been many viral sequences that these were trained on, and that single-strand DNA genomes overall are rather under-reported. But no matter the analysis or annotation, at least 25% of the damaging mutations cannot at present have any mechanism assigned to them. So even as well-studied a system as this bacteriophage still has a lot of blank areas and black boxes in it, a situation the authors describe as “rather humbling”. But you could apply that phrase to biology as a whole and only a fool would argue with you.
